parts.title: How Well Do Long-Lasting HIV Injections Work, and How Long Do People Stay on Them? A Look at Migrants Living With HIV in Spain, Part of the RELATIVITY Study
parts.abstract:
ABSTRACT

Introduction

Migrants living with HIV often move around a lot, can be more vulnerable, and may have little information about their HIV virus's genetic makeup (its genotype) or about the treatments they have had in the past. We wanted to find out how well a long-acting injection of two HIV medicines, cabotegravir and rilpivirine (together called CAB+RPV), works in migrants in Spain, and how long people stay on it.

Methods

We ran a study across 58 Spanish hospitals. It followed adults who had HIV, whose virus was already under control (virologically suppressed), and who had switched to the CAB+RPV injection before January 2025. We began collecting data in June 2023. We compared the starting details and the results of migrants with those of people born in Spain. To look for factors linked to virological failure (VF), meaning the virus coming back out of control, and to people stopping treatment, we used a statistical method called Cox proportional hazards regression. It looks at how the risk of an event changes over time while taking many other factors into account at once. We also used propensity score matching (PSM). This pairs people up so that the two groups are alike in gender, age, known genotype and any earlier virological failure, which helps remove the effect of other differences between them.

Results

Of 3135 people in the study, 951 (30.3%) were migrants, mostly from Latin America. The median follow-up was 13.8 months, meaning half the people were followed for longer than this and half for less. The middle half of people were followed for between 8.91 and 19.1 months (the interquartile range).

Virological failure happened in 0.9% of migrants and 0.5% of people born in Spain. The odds ratio was 1.89, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) of 0.69 to 5.03 and p = 0.22. An odds ratio compares how likely something is in one group against another. The confidence interval is the range of values that fit our data well. A p-value tells us how often a gap at least this large would turn up by chance alone if there were really no difference. A result is called statistically significant when p is below 0.05, meaning a gap this large would appear by chance less than 5% of the time.

In our adjusted models, which take other factors into account, migrants showed a trend towards more virological failure, but it was not statistically significant (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 2.16, 95% CI 0.89–5.22; p = 0.079). The adjusted hazard ratio compares how quickly an event happens in one group against another.

At 12 months, 95.8% of migrants (461/481) were still on the CAB+RPV injection, compared with 98.3% of people born in Spain (1348/1372) (p = 0.005). Migrants stopped treatment because of any side effect more often (3.3% vs. 1.8%). Being a migrant was significantly linked to stopping treatment because of side effects at the injection site (aHR 2.63, 95% CI 1.33–5.26; p = 0.005) and because of side effects elsewhere in the body (aHR 3.33, 95% CI 1.45–7.69, p = 0.005).

In the matched group (932 people in each group), being a migrant was linked to a higher risk of virological failure on its own (aHR 3.51, 95% CI 0.95–12.98, p = 0.045). It was also linked to stopping treatment because of side effects elsewhere in the body (aHR 2.88, 95% CI 1.01–8.17, p = 0.047).

Conclusions

Nearly one in three people who switched to the CAB+RPV injection were migrants. Virological failure was rare overall, but migrants had a significantly higher risk of stopping treatment, partly because of side effects. These findings show that migrants need closer monitoring and care plans designed for them, so that more of them stay on long-acting HIV injections.
parts.introduction_first:
Migrants are an important group of people living with HIV, both around the world and in Europe. In 2023, 11,837 people born outside the country where they were diagnosed with HIV were diagnosed in the European Economic Area. That was 47.9% of all new HIV cases there [1]. Most came from sub-Saharan Africa, Central and Eastern Europe, and Latin America.

Migrants living with HIV face several kinds of stigma at once, linked to HIV, to being a migrant, to race and to gender [2]. We do not have detailed information about how well these people move through the whole path of HIV care [3]. Even so, migrants often worry about keeping their jobs, face barriers to getting health care, and move around a lot, both inside and outside the country they live in. As a result, fewer people in vulnerable groups get HIV treatment (antiretroviral therapy, or ART), and fewer of them keep their virus under control. This is especially true for migrants without legal papers [4]. Studies show that migrants, especially those from sub-Saharan Africa, are more likely than the general population to stop their treatment, to fall out of contact with their care team, and to have their virus come back or their immune system weaken [5].
parts.conclusion:
5

Conclusions

Migrants made up almost one in three people who switched to the long-acting HIV injection. They kept up with their injection schedule about as well as people born in Spain. We had less information about the starting genotype and subtype of the HIV virus in migrants, yet virological failure was rare. However, migrants had a significantly higher risk of stopping the CAB+RPV injection, often because of side effects, both at the injection site and elsewhere in the body. These findings show that migrants need closer monitoring and care plans designed for them, so that more of them stay on long-acting HIV injections.
parts.introduction_rest:
In Spain, 49.8% of the 3196 people diagnosed with HIV in 2023 were born abroad, and two-thirds of those came from Latin America [6]. People from this group, including those from Venezuela, Colombia or Peru, face big barriers to getting care. Among asylum seekers, 21% had gaps in their treatment, and 33% lost control of their virus [7].

The CAB+RPV injection is the first long-acting HIV injection approved in Europe. It is injected into the muscle every 8 weeks. In clinical trials, it worked very well when people living with HIV whose virus was already under control switched from their usual treatment to it [8, 9]. Studies that followed groups of people in real-life settings have also confirmed that it is safe, works well and is acceptable to patients [10, 11, 12, 13]. Long-acting HIV injections can help people who find it hard to remember their daily pills. They can also help people who feel judged because of their HIV, or who grow tired of taking a pill every day for the rest of their lives [14, 15].

Some factors raise the risk of the virus coming back out of control. One is a body mass index (BMI) of 30 kg/m2 or more, which means a person weighs a lot for their height. Others are certain changes in the virus's genes that make it resistant to a family of HIV medicines called non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs). A third is a group of HIV virus types called A1/A6 [16]. However, the CARES study found that virological failure was rare in the A1 type, happening in only 0.8% of people [17].

Migrants may face a higher risk of virological failure for several reasons. More of their HIV virus types are non-B subtypes, meaning types other than the most common one, called B. They also move around a lot, can be vulnerable, and often have incomplete information about their earlier HIV genotype and treatment. Still, long-acting HIV injections may help migrants, because they fit better with work schedules and may reduce the stigma people feel.

For migrants, health care and social life are closely tied together. They move from place to place, their treatment histories are often broken up, and they are rarely included in clinical trials. All of this shows why new treatments such as the CAB+RPV injection need to be judged with fairness in mind, asking whether everyone gets a fair chance to benefit from good care. Making sure the benefits of treatment are shared fairly is essential.

In this study, we set out to compare how well the CAB+RPV injection works, and how long people stay on it, among migrants in Spain and among people born in Spain. We wanted to find out whether being a migrant is linked to higher rates of virological failure or of stopping treatment, so that care can be designed to meet migrants' needs.
parts.methods:
2

Methods

2.1

How We Set Up the Study and Where It Took Place

The RELATIVITY study is a large study carried out across Spain, in 58 real-world hospitals and clinics. It is a prospective cohort study, which means we followed the same group of people forward in time. Our aim was to find out how well the long-acting HIV injection of cabotegravir and rilpivirine (CAB+RPV) works, and how safe it is. The study began in June 2023, although the injection had already been on sale in Spain since December 2022. We expect to keep monitoring it until 2029. We included patients who switched to the CAB+RPV injection before January 2025.

We collected information in two ways. For the time before a patient's hospital joined the study and before the patient signed an informed consent form, we looked back at existing records. From that point on, we collected information as it happened. The full data have been published elsewhere [18]. Here we present a smaller study within the RELATIVITY group, which we call a substudy. It looks at how well the injection works and how long people stay on it in migrants, and compares this with people born in Spain who live with HIV. We used the everyday meaning of "migrant" as someone born outside Spain, which matches how Spain's national HIV reports use the word.

2.2

Who Took Part

We invited adults aged 18 or older who had HIV and whose virus was already under control. To count, a person had to have received at least one dose of the CAB+RPV injection before January 2025. When treatment started, their viral load had to be undetectable, meaning below 50 copies of the virus's genetic material (RNA) in each millilitre of blood. We did not include people who were pregnant, or who had already taken part in a clinical trial of the CAB+RPV injection. We left out pregnant women because neither the medicine's official label nor current European or Spanish guidelines recommend the injection during pregnancy. We split the participants into two main groups based on where they were born: migrants and people born in Spain.

For our main analysis, we used everyone in the study group, and all of them had an undetectable viral load (below 50 copies/mL) when they started the CAB+RPV injection. We also ran a second analysis using only people who met the conditions in the official label for starting the injection. We call this the on-label group. To be in it, a person had to have an undetectable viral load. They also had to have no resistance-associated mutations (RAMs) to two families of HIV medicines, integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs) and non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs). These are genetic changes in the virus that can make certain medicines stop working. Finally, they had to have had no earlier virological failure with either of these two families of medicines.

2.3

How We Collected Information

We stored and handled the study data in REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), an online system for recording research data, hosted at Infanta Leonor University Hospital [19]. We collected information about each person's background, their body measurements, their HIV, their lab results and their treatment. The treatment information included the injection schedule, the type of injection, where it was given, and any short-term daily pills used between injections (called oral bridge therapy). We also recorded follow-up. There was no fixed follow-up timetable. Each hospital followed its own usual way of checking patients, in line with national and international guidelines.

2.4

What We Measured

We recorded each person's background, other health conditions, use of substances such as drugs, weight and body mass index (BMI, a measure of weight compared with height). We also recorded when they were diagnosed with HIV, the HIV treatments they had had before, any virological failure and any earlier blips. A blip is a short-lived, small rise in the amount of virus in the blood. When available, we also recorded the HIV-1 subtype and the genotype resistance testing, which checks the virus's genetic makeup for changes that could make medicines stop working.

We defined a viral blip as a short-lived, low rise in HIV-1 RNA (50–200 copies/mL) that went back to undetectable levels without any change to the treatment. We defined virological failure as either two HIV-1 RNA measurements in a row of 200 copies/mL or more, or a single measurement above 500 copies/mL that led to the treatment being stopped.

Our main result was whether people were still on the injection at 12 months. Our other results were whether the virus stayed under control (below 50 copies/mL), virological failure, measures of the immune system, how well people kept up with their injection schedule, and the reasons they stopped treatment. We measured how well people kept up with their injections as the share of days covered. A dose counted as on time if it was given within 7 days either side of the planned date in the 8-week schedule. We defined staying on treatment as the time from starting the HIV treatment until the person stopped it for good. We measured everything in the everyday care setting of each hospital that took part.

2.5

How We Analysed the Data

For things that fall into categories, such as reasons for stopping treatment, we give the number of people and the percentage. For measurements such as age, we give the median (the middle value) and the interquartile range (the range covering the middle half of people). We chose this way of showing the data because a check called the Kolmogorov–Smirnov or Shapiro–Wilk test showed that, in every case, the values did not follow the usual bell-shaped pattern.

To compare the two groups, we used the Chi-square test or Fisher's exact test for categories. These tests check whether the share of people in each category differs between the groups more than chance would usually produce. For measurements, we used the independent samples t-test or the Mann–Whitney U test, depending on the data.

We drew Kaplan–Meier survival curves. These are graphs that show, over time, the chance of still being free of virological failure, side effects or other reasons for stopping treatment. We compared migrants with people born in Spain using the log-rank test, which checks whether the two curves differ.

To measure how other factors were linked to the time until an event, we used Cox proportional hazards regression. We report the results as adjusted hazard ratios (aHR), with 95% confidence intervals (CI) and p-values. Every Cox model included a wide set of factors that might affect the results: age and gender at the start, nationality, earlier virological failure, whether the virus had shown resistance to HIV medicines before, and a long list of other health conditions at the start.

This method assumes that the gap in risk between the groups stays about the same over time. We checked this by looking at graphs of a measure called Schoenfeld residuals and by running a formal test. Neither showed any sign that the assumption was broken. We judged how well the models worked using the concordance index, which shows how well a model's predictions agree with what actually happened. A likelihood ratio test confirmed that the models as a whole were statistically significant.

We used propensity score matching (PSM) to remove the effect of other differences between the groups. We matched people by gender, age, known genotype and earlier virological failure. To check that the groups were well balanced, we calculated standardized mean differences before and after matching. This is a measure of how far apart the two groups' averages are, and we treated values below 0.1 as showing good balance. We did not fill in any missing data with estimates. The register behind this study group is very complete, and the missing information was only clinical details that were not in the patients' medical records.

We also ran a second analysis that included only people living with HIV whose prescription followed the official technical sheet. This left out people whose virus had changes (mutations) in the genes for NNRTIs or INSTIs, and we call this the on-label group. We did all the analyses in R version 4.4.0 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria).

2.6

Ethics

The Ethics Committee for Research with Medicines of the Burgos and Soria Health Area approved the study plan (code 23–00144). Every patient received an information sheet and gave written informed consent before joining. We kept the data confidential, following Spanish and European Union rules on protecting personal data.
parts.discussion:
4

Discussion

In our study, migrants living with HIV who switched to the long-acting HIV injection of cabotegravir and rilpivirine (CAB+RPV) had low rates of virological failure, meaning their virus came back out of control. These rates were similar to those seen in the main clinical trials that tested the injection. However, migrants stopped treatment more often than people born in Spain, partly because of side effects at the injection site and side effects elsewhere in the body. These findings suggest that how long people stay on a treatment depends on many things. It is not only about how well the medicine works. It also depends on the medical care, on how health services are organised, and on what patients experience.

Let us start with virological failure. We used a definition that matches recent expert agreement [20]. With it, virological failure happened in 1% or fewer of migrants, similar to what clinical trials and other studies of people in everyday care have reported [12, 13, 21].

An important point is that the virus was already under control when people switched. In that situation, not knowing the starting genotype (the HIV virus's genetic makeup) did not seem to harm how well or how safely the CAB+RPV injection worked [22]. For migrants, the starting genotype was harder to find. This reflects real-life limits, such as people having been diagnosed or cared for in other countries. Without this information, we cannot judge how risky the virus was at the start, or whether the virus had become resistant to the medicine.

We also did not know whether 17% of migrants had had virological failure before. That means nearly one in five started the CAB+RPV injection without any record of earlier HIV treatment. Even so, migrants did as well as people born in Spain when it came to virological failure. In Spain, HIV treatment is available to everyone, people have social protection, and HIV care is part of specialist units. These things likely help make the treatment work very well once patients are in care.

There is another reason. In everyday practice, doctors usually choose who gets the CAB+RPV injection based on their medical situation. This may have meant that our group included people whose virus was already steadily under control and who had a regular follow-up, whatever their origin.

Importantly, these findings do not mean that migrants are not vulnerable because of the way society and health care are organised. The RELATIVITY study did not systematically collect key social and practical details, such as legal status, housing, problems with keeping a job, or health literacy (how well people understand health information).

Among migrants who had virological failure, we found three things. They had a higher body mass index (BMI, a measure of weight compared with height) at the start. They had a higher HIV viral load (the amount of virus in the blood) when they were diagnosed. And they had more viral blips in the 5 years before the switch. A viral blip is a short-lived rise in the amount of virus in the blood. This fits with evidence that people whose virus does not stay under control often had other problems beforehand, such as a high viral load before treatment or a virus that was not fully controlled on tablets [23]. Because of the limits in our data, we could not find specific social or practical factors that predicted virological failure. Other studies, however, have found that younger age and being unemployed are important risk factors for migrants [24].

Among people who had virological failure, the virus often became resistant to integrase inhibitors (INSTIs), the family of HIV medicines that CAB+RPV belongs to. This has also been reported elsewhere [25]. Studies that combine the results of many trials show that switching to the CAB+RPV injection carries a higher risk of new resistance than taking two or three HIV medicines as tablets. However, this increase was not statistically significant [26]. Most patients who stop working well on the injection can get their virus under control again with a single tablet taken by mouth [27]. In our study, though, fewer people got their virus under control again than we expected, likely because we followed them for only a short time. Future studies should look at this again.

Migrants may find it harder to keep up with the steps of HIV care. This can affect how well they take their treatment, whether they stay in care, and how well their virus responds [28]. Around the world, migrants do not always have equal access to HIV treatment, which leads to unfair differences in care. Sometimes undocumented migrants have limited access [29]. Yet migrants often face more barriers to staying in care than to getting treatment in the first place. A review of the path of HIV care found that 68% of migrants reported barriers to staying in care, compared with 30% for getting into care. Two-thirds of these barriers were personal problems, such as unmet basic needs (housing, money, work commitments or mental health), which raise the risk of falling out of contact with care [30].

Across many kinds of tablet treatment, migrants generally stop treatment more often [5]. In our study, though, migrants and people born in Spain kept up with their treatment about equally well. We measured this as the percentage of days covered, meaning the share of days on which a person had taken their medicine. This shows that once migrants started the injection, they kept up with the injection schedule well.

Even so, migrants stopped treatment because of side effects twice as often as people born in Spain. As far as we know, no one has reported this elsewhere. Stopping because of side effects at the injection site was significantly higher in migrants, especially in the group whose injection was given exactly as the official instructions say. Studies that combine many trials show that CAB+RPV carries a higher risk of stopping because of side effects than tablet treatments such as bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide or dolutegravir/abacavir/lamivudine [26]. So how well people tolerate the medicine is a top concern when switching treatments.

Migrant workers often work longer hours and in more physically demanding jobs. This may make them more likely to stop because of pain at the injection site. How the injection is given may also affect side effects. This includes the injection technique, the staff's experience, the needle length, how injections into the buttocks are done, and how the clinic works. Possible genetic factors may play a part too. No particular side effect elsewhere in the body was more common in migrants, but women seemed to be affected more than their share would suggest.

The RELATIVITY study did not record people's travel history or whether they went back to their home countries. This matters a lot, because travel can make the virus come back [31]. For migrants on the long-acting HIV injection, travel may affect whether they stay on treatment in two ways. The injection may help them keep up with their treatment while travelling. But because the injections must be given at fixed times, frequent travellers may be more likely to miss an appointment. Doctors should think about care plans designed for these people, such as longer clinic hours, a short course of tablets to cover travel, and standard ways of managing pain, to help them stay on treatment.

The CAB+RPV injection has worked well even in people with HIV who have complicated medical needs, social difficulties, unstable housing, mental illness, drug or alcohol use, or a history of not taking their treatment [32]. This includes people whose virus could still be detected in their blood when they switched [33, 34]. So migrants with complicated social situations are likely to benefit from this treatment. The CAB+RPV injection is also good value for money in our setting [35] and helps reach the UNAIDS 95-95-95 goals [36]. These goals aim for 95% of people living with HIV to know their status, 95% of those to be on treatment, and 95% of those to have their virus under control.

Our study has limitations. We looked both at people who had switched before the study began and at people who switched during it. This kind of design can be affected by who ends up in the study and by gaps or errors in the information. The quality of older records also varied. This was especially true for some people's side effects soon after switching, their past viral blips or treatment failures, and whether their starting genotype was available. These problems may limit how reliable our results are, how well they apply to other groups, and how firmly we can say one thing causes another. However, everyone in the study was already being actively followed when they joined, so we could reliably record the main outcomes.

The median follow-up was short, so we cannot judge how long the treatment's benefits last, look for rare side effects, or spot virological failures that happen late. Also, most people had the most common HIV virus subtype (B), and only a few had other subtypes, especially A6. This limits how well we can judge the risks for each subtype.

A key limitation is that we did not collect information about people's social and mental situation or about how society and health care are organised. This includes legal status, stable housing, problems with keeping a job, level of education, and how people came to Spain. Without it, we cannot firmly say that being a migrant causes people to stop treatment, especially when they stopped because of side effects. Also, the year people arrived in Spain was not recorded in the same way at every hospital, so we could not study it. Even so, the time since arrival may affect how vulnerable people are, how involved they are in care, and how long they stay on treatment. In future updates, we aim to add organised information about people's social and economic situation.

Finally, care was probably handled differently at different hospitals, but patients were treated following national and European guidelines, which limited these differences. The study's strengths are that it was large, took place across the whole country in many hospitals, included a varied group of people in everyday care, and used propensity score matching to take other differences between the groups into account.

Our findings give important real-world evidence that the CAB+RPV injection works well in migrants living with HIV in Spain. They show that migrants, who often face social, practical and medical difficulties, have their own particular challenges with long-acting HIV injections. Tackling these differences is essential for giving the best possible care and for fairer health [37]. It makes sure that everyone, and especially the most vulnerable groups, benefits equally from new treatments.

Results

3.1

Who Took Part

The RELATIVITY study included 3192 people who switched to the long-acting HIV injection of cabotegravir plus rilpivine (CAB+RPV) before January 2025. Of these, 3135 met our rules for taking part. Of those 3135, 951 (30.3%) were migrants. Most of the migrants (766, or 80.5% of them) came from Latin America. Smaller numbers came from Africa (63, 6.6%) and Western Europe (51, 5.4%). Figure 1 and File S1 (Table S1) show where each migrant came from.

FIGURE 1

Countries of origin of the migrants who switched to the long-acting HIV injection of cabotegravir plus rilpivine in the RELATIVITY study, Spain. PWH: people living with HIV.

The starting details of migrants and of people born in Spain were different, as Table 1 shows. Migrants were younger. Their median age was 39.8 years, compared with 47.6 years for people born in Spain (p < 0.001). A larger share of migrants were cisgender women, meaning women whose gender identity matches the sex they were born with: 18.2% of migrants, compared with 13.3% of people born in Spain (p = 0.001). Migrants had also been on HIV treatment (antiretroviral therapy, or ART) for fewer years before switching to the injection: a median of 7 years, compared with 10 years (p < 0.001). Fewer migrants had a recorded history of virological failure (VF), meaning the virus coming back out of control: 2.1% of migrants, compared with 4.1% of people born in Spain (p = 0.004). The reasons people gave for switching did not differ between the two groups.

We had less information about resistance testing before the switch in migrants: 40.2% of migrants had it, compared with 49.4% of people born in Spain (p < 0.001). Resistance testing looks for changes in the HIV virus's genetic makeup (mutations) that can make it harder for medicines to work. Among the people who had this test, most had no mutations we could detect, and the share was similar in both groups: 84.3% of migrants and 85.6% of people born in Spain (p = 0.56).

We also looked at the different families of HIV medicines. Integrase inhibitors (INSTIs) are the family that includes cabotegravir. Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) are another family, and nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) are a third. Migrants and people born in Spain had similar rates of mutations that affect INSTIs: 2.1% of migrants versus 0.9% of people born in Spain (p = 0.101). Mutations that affect NNRTIs were found in 9.9% of migrants versus 8.2% of people born in Spain (p = 0.34). Only one of them, called E138A, was statistically significantly more common in migrants. 3.2.1

How Well the Virus Stayed Under Control

Virological failure was rare in both groups, and the difference between migrants and people born in Spain was not statistically significant. It happened in 0.9% of migrants and 0.5% of people born in Spain (odds ratio 1.89, 95% confidence interval 0.69–5.03; p = 0.22).

We also used a Kaplan–Meier analysis (Figure 2). This method follows how the chance of an event builds up over time. It showed no significant difference between the groups in the chance of virological failure over time (log-rank p = 0.86).

Next, we used a Cox proportional hazards model that took many other factors into account at once. In this model, being a migrant showed a significant trend towards more virological failure (adjusted hazard ratio 2.16, 95% confidence interval 0.89–5.22; p = 0.079). However, this result was limited by the small number of failures and by how uncertain the estimate was (File S2, Table S2).

3.2.2

What Was Linked to Virological Failure in Migrants

Table 4 describes the people in our study who had virological failure, including any new resistance mutations they developed. Among migrants, virological failure was linked to a higher body mass index (BMI) at the start and to a higher HIV viral load when they were diagnosed. A viral load is the amount of HIV virus in the blood. People who had virological failure were also more often those who had had at least three blips in the 5 years before switching to the CAB+RPV injection (Table 5). A blip is a short-lived rise in the viral load that comes back down again.

3.2.3

Staying on Treatment and Keeping Up With Injections

The median follow-up for the whole group was 13.8 months, with the middle half of people followed for between 8.91 and 19.1 months. Overall, people kept up with their CAB+RPV injections very well. The share of people who covered fewer than 90% of their injection days was similar in both groups: 1.4% of migrants and 1.8% of people born in Spain, and the difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.54).

However, fewer migrants stayed on the injection at both 6 and 12 months. At 6 months, 93.3% of migrants (706/757) were still on it, compared with 96.1% of people born in Spain (1844/1919) (p = 0.003). At 12 months, 95.8% of migrants (461/481) were still on it, compared with 98.3% of people born in Spain (1348/1372) (p = 0.005). Migrants also stopped the injection for a while more often: 1.8% of migrants, compared with 0.6% of people born in Spain (p = 0.005).

Among people who stopped the CAB+RPV injection, side effects were the most common reason. Migrants stopped because of any side effect more often (3.4% of migrants, compared with 1.8% of people born in Spain; p = 0.003). Table 3 shows the other reasons.

Figure 2 shows Kaplan–Meier curves for the time to key events, split by the reason people stopped treatment. We also used a Cox proportional hazards model that took many other factors into account, to look for what predicted stopping treatment because of side effects (File S2, Table S2). Three things were linked to stopping because of side effects elsewhere in the body: being older (each extra year of age: adjusted hazard ratio 1.05, 95% confidence interval 1.01–1.09, p = 0.015), being a woman (adjusted hazard ratio 2.63, 95% confidence interval 1.16–5.88, p = 0.021) and being a migrant (adjusted hazard ratio 3.33, 95% confidence interval 1.45–7.69, p = 0.005). Reactions at the injection site were significantly linked to being a migrant (adjusted hazard ratio 2.63, 95% confidence interval 1.33–5.26; p = 0.005) and to high blood pressure (adjusted hazard ratio 2.48, 95% confidence interval 1.07–5.71; p = 0.034).

3.3

Results After Matching People Up

Other differences between the groups could have affected our results. To take these into account, we used propensity score matching. This pairs each migrant with one person born in Spain who is alike in gender, age, whether the starting genotype was available, and any history of virological failure. This gave us 932 people in each group (File S3, Tables S3.1–S3.4).

In this matched group, virological failure was still rare. In the simple comparison, it did not differ significantly between migrants and people born in Spain (1% vs. 0.3%; odds ratio 3.02, 95% confidence interval 0.75–17.38; p = 0.15). However, migrants stopped treatment for good more often (9% of migrants, compared with 5.1% of people born in Spain; odds ratio 1.85, 95% confidence interval 1.26–2.72; p = 0.001).

File S3, Figure S3 shows Kaplan–Meier curves for the time to virological failure and to stopping treatment in the matched group, split by the specific reason. In this case, migrants stopped treatment more often in every category. There was also a borderline significant trend towards more virological failure in migrants (adjusted hazard ratio 3.51, 95% confidence interval 0.95–12.98, p = 0.045). However, this result is quite uncertain, because so few people had virological failure.

3.4

Results for People Treated as the Medicine Is Meant to Be Used

We also ran a second analysis that included only people living with HIV whose prescription followed the official instructions for the medicine. It left out people who had mutations that affect NNRTIs or INSTIs. The results are in File S4, Tables S4.1–S4.4 and Figure S4.
